title: Ἡρακλῆς καὶ Πλοῦτος
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 130 (= Perry 111). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ἡρακλῆς ἰσοθεωθεὶς καὶ παρὰ Διὶ ἑστιώμενος ἕνα ἕκαστον τῶν θεῶν μετὰ πολλῆς φιλοφροσύνης ἠσπάζετο.
sentences.tr: Hēraklēs isotheōtheis kai para Dii hestiōmenos hena hekaston tōn theōn meta pollēs philophrosynēs ēspazeto.
sentences.l: Heracles, having been made equal to the gods and being feasted at Zeus's, greeted each one of the gods with great friendliness.
sentences.n: ἰσοθεόω is a rare verb built straight from ἰσόθεος, 'equal to a god': it names Heracles' passage from man to god after the pyre on Oeta, which is why he is a guest at this table at all. παρά with the dative is 'at the house of'. ἕνα ἕκαστον is 'one each', that is, each singly and in turn.

sentences.t: Καὶ δὴ τελευταίου εἰσελθόντος τοῦ Πλούτου, κατὰ τοῦ ἐδάφους κύψας ἀπεστρέψατο αὐτόν.
sentences.tr: Kai dē teleutaiou eiselthontos tou Ploutou, kata tou edaphous kypsas apestrepsato auton.
sentences.l: And in fact, Plutus having come in last, he stooped toward the floor and turned away from him.
sentences.i: And when Plutus came in last of all, Heracles stooped toward the floor and turned his back on him.
sentences.n: Πλοῦτος is Wealth itself, made a person and given a place at the table. Another genitive absolute, with τελευταίου standing predicatively: it was last that he came in. κατά with the genitive is direction downward, so 'down toward the floor'. ἀποστρέφομαι in the middle takes the accusative of the one turned away from; with the stoop toward the floor it withholds the greeting Heracles has just given everyone else.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ Ζεὺς θαυμάσας τὸ γεγονὸς ἐπυνθάνετο αὐτοῦ τὴν αἰτίαν δι’ ἣν πάντας τοὺς δαίμονας προσαγορεύσας ἀσμένως μόνον τὸν Πλοῦτον ὑποβλέπεται.
sentences.tr: Ho de Zeus thaumasas to gegonos epynthaneto autou tēn aitian di’ hēn pantas tous daimonas prosagoreusas asmenōs monon ton Plouton hypobleptetai.
sentences.l: And Zeus, having wondered at what had happened, asked him the reason for which, having greeted all the divinities gladly, he looks askance at Plutus alone.
sentences.i: And Zeus, astonished at what had happened, asked him the reason why, when he had greeted all the divinities gladly, he looked askance at Plutus alone.
sentences.n: τὸ γεγονός is the perfect participle used as a noun, 'the thing that has come about'. ὑποβλέπομαι is to look from under the brows, the sidelong look of dislike or suspicion. The present ὑποβλέπεται is kept after the past main verb: Greek leaves an indirect question in the tense the speaker's own words would have had, where English shifts it back.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ εἶπεν· « Ἀλλ’ ἔγωγε διὰ τοῦτο αὐτὸν ὑποβλέπομαι ὅτι παρ’ ὃν καιρὸν ἐν ἀνθρώποις ἤμην, ἑώρων αὐτὸν ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ πλεῖστον τοῖς πονηροῖς συνόντα. »
sentences.tr: Ho de eipen· « All’ egōge dia touto auton hypoblepomai hoti par’ hon kairon en anthrōpois ēmēn, heōrōn auton hōs epi to pleiston tois ponērois synonta. »
sentences.l: And he said: « Well, I for my part look askance at him for this reason, that during the time I was among men, I used to see him for the most part keeping company with the wicked. »
sentences.n: παρ’ ὃν καιρόν is παρά with the accusative of time extended alongside, 'through the time in which'. ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ πλεῖστον is a set phrase, 'for the most part'. συνόντα is a supplementary participle after ἑώρων — what he saw Plutus doing, not merely that he saw him; σύνειμι with the dative is to keep company with.

sentences.t: Ὁ λόγος λεχθείη ἂν ἐπ’ ἀνδρὸς πλουσίου μὲν τὴν τύχην, πονηροῦ δὲ τὸν τρόπον.
sentences.tr: Ho logos lechtheiē an ep’ andros plousiou men tēn tychēn, ponērou de ton tropon.
sentences.l: The story might be told of a man rich in his fortune but wicked in his ways.
sentences.n: λεχθείη ἄν is the potential optative, the mild 'might, could'. τὴν τύχην and τὸν τρόπον are accusatives of respect, each hung on its own genitive adjective and the two held apart by μέν and δέ: rich as regards his luck, wicked as regards his manner of life. ἐπί with the genitive here is 'in the case of'.
